summary: Defines a Telnet option that disables the exchange of go-ahead signals between the Telnet modules. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of saying over after every turn, both sides can talk freely. This option turns the over signal off.

questions: what is telnet suppress go ahead
subtitle: A Telnet option that turns off the half-duplex 'over' signal for connections that can talk both ways at once.

tldr.problem: The Network Virtual Terminal nominally follows a half-duplex protocol with a GO AHEAD signal, which is an unneeded burden on a full-duplex connection between a full-duplex terminal and a suitable host.
tldr.mechanism: The SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD option (code 3) lets each direction agree that the sender need not transmit GO AHEAD (GA) characters.
tldr.outcome: With the option in effect, a received IAC GA is treated as a no-op, and the sender should transmit characters as soon as possible.

today: RFC 858 is an Internet Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Suppress Go Ahead
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) nominally follows a half-duplex protocol complete with a GO AHEAD (GA) signal. There is no reason to burden a full-duplex connection, between a full-duplex terminal and a host built for full-duplex terminals, with that signal.

So the RFC defines a Telnet option, SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD (code 3), with which the parties agree that one or both should suppress sending GAs.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way made each side say 'over' when finished. If both can talk at once, that is a waste, so this lets them skip it.

sections.title: The Four Commands
sections.content:
The option uses the standard negotiation commands:

  • IAC WILL SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD: the sender requests permission to begin suppressing GAs, or confirms it now will.
  • IAC WON'T SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD: the sender demands to begin, or continue, transmitting GA with data.
  • IAC DO SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD: the sender requests that the data sender start suppressing GA, or confirms that it is expected to.
  • IAC DON'T SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD: the sender demands that the receiver start or continue transmitting GAs.

The default is WON'T and DON'T, so go aheads are transmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side can ask 'may we skip saying over?' or insist 'no, keep saying it'. Unless they agree, the 'over' stays.

sections.title: What Changes on the Wire
sections.content:
When the option is in effect between a sender of data and its receiver, the sender need not transmit GAs. The parties will probably suppress GO AHEAD in both directions if they do at all, but it must be suppressed in each direction independently.

With the option in effect, a received IAC GA should be treated as a NOP (no operation), although IAC GA should not normally be sent in this mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Once 'over' is switched off, if someone says it anyway, the listener just ignores it.

sections.title: Implementation Advice
sections.content:
Because the option is something like the opposite of a line-at-a-time mode, a sender that is suppressing GO AHEADs should try to transmit characters as soon as possible, with minimal buffering, consistent with any other agreements in effect.

Many Telnet implementations will want to couple SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD to the ECHO option, so that when echo is in effect, suppress-go-ahead is too. Both normally have to be in effect to get what is commonly understood as character-at-a-time echoing by the remote computer.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are not waiting to say 'over', send each letter right away instead of saving them up. Pairing it with the echo setting makes typing feel instant.
